linear_algebra.subject: Advanced Mathematics
clues: I am the branch of mathematics studying vectors, matrices, and linear transformations.
I provide the mathematical language for solving large systems of equations.
Row reduction and Gaussian elimination are my key techniques.
I describe transformations of space through matrix operations.
Computer graphics, physics, and data science all rely heavily on me.

educationalInfo.definition: The branch of mathematics dealing with vector spaces, linear transformations, matrices, and systems of linear equations.
educationalInfo.commonMistakes: Treating matrix multiplication as commutative (AB ≠ BA in general). Errors in Gaussian elimination steps.
educationalInfo.funFact: Google's PageRank algorithm is a linear algebra problem involving a matrix of over a trillion entries.
practiceQuestions: Solve the system: x+y=5, 2x−y=1 using matrix methods.
What is the rank of the identity matrix?

linear_algebra.hint: Recall that Linear Algebra refers to: The branch of mathematics dealing with vector spaces, linear transformations, matrices, and systems of linear equations.

logarithms.name: Logarithms
logarithms.subject: Advanced Mathematics
clues: I am the inverse of exponentiation.
logₐ(b) = c means aᶜ = b.
log(a×b) = log(a) + log(b) is one of my key laws.
I can convert exponential equations into linear ones.
log₁₀(1000) = 3 because 10³ = 1000.

educationalInfo.definition: The logarithm logₐ(x) answers: 'To what power must a be raised to get x?' It is the inverse of aˣ.
educationalInfo.commonMistakes: Thinking log(a+b) = log(a) + log(b) (incorrect). Confusing natural log (ln) with log base 10.
educationalInfo.funFact: John Napier invented logarithms in 1614 to simplify the astronomical calculations navigators needed: multiplications became additions.

logarithms.hint: Recall that Logarithms refers to: The logarithm logₐ(x) answers: 'To what power must a be raised to get x?' It is the inverse of aˣ.

binomial_theorem.name: Binomial Theorem
binomial_theorem.subject: Advanced Mathematics
clues: I expand expressions of the form (a + b)ⁿ for any positive integer n.
My coefficients come from Pascal's Triangle.
The general term of my expansion is ⁿCᵣ × aⁿ⁻ʳ × bʳ.
(a+b)² = a² + 2ab + b² is the simplest case of me.
I am used in probability, combinatorics, and approximation theory.

educationalInfo.definition: The Binomial Theorem states: (a+b)ⁿ = Σ(r=0 to n) ⁿCᵣ aⁿ⁻ʳ bʳ.
educationalInfo.commonMistakes: Errors in computing ⁿCᵣ. Using the wrong term number for the general term.
educationalInfo.funFact: Pascal's Triangle, which gives Binomial coefficients, was known to Chinese mathematician Jia Xian 500 years before Pascal.
practiceQuestions: Find the coefficient of x² in (1+x)⁵.

binomial_theorem.hint: Recall that Binomial Theorem refers to: The Binomial Theorem states: (a+b)ⁿ = Σ(r=0 to n) ⁿCᵣ aⁿ⁻ʳ bʳ.

permutations_combinations.name: Permutations & Combinations
permutations_combinations.subject: Advanced Mathematics
clues: I count the number of ways to arrange or select objects.
When order matters, I use permutations: nPr = n!/(n−r)!.
When order does not matter, I use combinations: nCr = n!/(r!(n−r)!).
Choosing 3 books from 5 regardless of order uses nCr.
Arranging 4 people in 4 seats uses 4! = 24 permutations.

educationalInfo.definition: Permutation counts ordered arrangements; combination counts unordered selections. nPr = n!/(n−r)!, nCr = n!/(r!(n−r)!).
examples: Number of ways to deal 5 cards from 52: 52C5 = 2,598,960
educationalInfo.commonMistakes: Using permutation when order doesn't matter. Forgetting that 0! = 1.
educationalInfo.funFact: The number of possible chess games after 40 moves exceeds 10¹²⁰: far more than atoms in the observable universe.
practiceQuestions: In how many ways can 3 students be chosen from 8?
How many 4-letter arrangements can be made from the letters of MATHS?

permutations_combinations.hint: Recall that Permutations & Combinations refers to: Permutation counts ordered arrangements; combination counts unordered selections.

coordinate_geometry.name: Coordinate Geometry
coordinate_geometry.subject: Coordinate & Calculus
clues: I study geometric figures using algebraic equations and a coordinate plane.
I calculate distances, midpoints, and gradients between points.
The distance between (x₁,y₁) and (x₂,y₂) is √((x₂−x₁)²+(y₂−y₁)²).
I can determine whether lines are parallel, perpendicular, or intersecting.
René Descartes invented my coordinate framework in the 17th century.

educationalInfo.definition: The study of geometry using a coordinate system to describe and analyse shapes algebraically.
educationalInfo.commonMistakes: Forgetting to square before adding in the distance formula. Confusing gradient with y-intercept.
educationalInfo.funFact: Coordinate geometry bridges algebra and geometry: Descartes said it came to him in a dream while watching a fly on his ceiling.
practiceQuestions: Find the midpoint of the segment joining (−3,5) and (7,−1).

coordinate_geometry.hint: Recall that Coordinate Geometry refers to: The study of geometry using a coordinate system to describe and analyse shapes algebraically.

line_equation.name: Line Equation
line_equation.subject: Coordinate & Calculus
clues: I describe a straight line on the coordinate plane.
My most common form is y = mx + c, where m is gradient and c is y-intercept.
Given two points, I can always be determined uniquely.
Two lines with equal gradients are parallel.
Two lines with gradients m₁ and m₂ are perpendicular if m₁ × m₂ = −1.

educationalInfo.definition: The equation of a straight line, typically written as y = mx + c (gradient-intercept form) or ax + by + c = 0.
educationalInfo.commonMistakes: Mixing up gradient with y-intercept. Computing gradient as run/rise instead of rise/run.
educationalInfo.funFact: Every straight line can be expressed in the form ax+by=c: even vertical lines (x=k) just have b=0.
practiceQuestions: Find the equation of the line through (2,5) with gradient 3.
Find the gradient of the line perpendicular to y = 4x − 7.

line_equation.hint: Recall that Line Equation refers to: The equation of a straight line, typically written as y = mx + c (gradient-intercept form) or ax + by + c = 0.

section_formula.name: Section Formula
section_formula.subject: Coordinate & Calculus
clues: I find the coordinates of a point that divides a line segment in a given ratio.
For internal division in ratio m:n, I give x = (mx₂+nx₁)/(m+n).
The midpoint formula is my special case when m = n = 1.
I can also handle external division, where the point lies outside the segment.
If P divides AB in ratio 2:3, I calculate exactly where P lies.

educationalInfo.definition: The section formula gives the coordinates of a point dividing a segment joining (x₁,y₁) and (x₂,y₂) in ratio m:n.
educationalInfo.commonMistakes: Swapping m and n. Confusing internal and external division.
educationalInfo.funFact: The section formula generalises to 3D and is used in computer graphics for interpolating between keyframes in animation.
practiceQuestions: Find the point dividing (2,−3) and (8,9) in ratio 1:2.
Find the centroid of the triangle with vertices (1,2),(3,6),(5,0).

section_formula.hint: Recall that Section Formula refers to: The section formula gives the coordinates of a point dividing a segment joining (x₁,y₁) and (x₂,y₂) in ratio m:n.

conic_sections.name: Conic Sections
conic_sections.subject: Coordinate & Calculus
clues: I am the family of curves formed by slicing a cone with a plane.
My four main members are circle, ellipse, parabola, and hyperbola.
A circle is my special case when the slice is perfectly horizontal.
A parabola is the path of a projectile under gravity.
My general second-degree equation is ax²+bxy+cy²+dx+ey+f=0.

educationalInfo.definition: Curves formed by the intersection of a plane with a right circular cone: circle, ellipse, parabola, hyperbola.
educationalInfo.commonMistakes: Misidentifying conic type from its equation. Forgetting to complete the square to find centre/vertex.
educationalInfo.funFact: Planets orbit the Sun in ellipses: discovered by Kepler in 1609 using conic section mathematics developed by Apollonius 1800 years earlier.

conic_sections.hint: Recall that Conic Sections refers to: Curves formed by the intersection of a plane with a right circular cone: circle, ellipse, parabola, hyperbola.

limits.name: Limits
limits.subject: Coordinate & Calculus
clues: I describe the value a function approaches as the input gets close to a specific value.
I am the foundation of calculus.
lim(x→2) of x² = 4 is a simple example of me.
I can handle cases where the function is undefined at the exact point.
L'Hôpital's Rule helps evaluate me in 0/0 or ∞/∞ indeterminate forms.

educationalInfo.definition: lim(x→a) f(x) = L means f(x) can be made arbitrarily close to L by taking x sufficiently close to a.
educationalInfo.commonMistakes: Assuming the limit equals the function value (it may not exist or differ). Mis-applying L'Hôpital when form isn't 0/0 or ∞/∞.
educationalInfo.funFact: Newton and Leibniz both invented calculus independently: the limit concept was only rigorously formalised by Cauchy and Weierstrass 150 years later.

limits.hint: Recall that Limits refers to: lim(x→a) f(x) = L means f(x) can be made arbitrarily close to L by taking x sufficiently close to a.

differentiation.name: Differentiation
differentiation.subject: Coordinate & Calculus
clues: I find the instantaneous rate of change of a function.
I produce the derivative, often written as dy/dx or f'(x).
The power rule: d/dx(xⁿ) = nxⁿ⁻¹ is my simplest rule.
I find the gradient of a tangent to a curve at any point.
Setting my result equal to zero locates maxima and minima of a curve.

educationalInfo.definition: The process of finding the derivative of a function, representing its instantaneous rate of change.
educationalInfo.commonMistakes: Forgetting to bring the power down as a coefficient. Not reducing the power by 1.
educationalInfo.funFact: Isaac Newton developed differentiation to explain planetary motion: he called it 'the method of fluxions'.
practiceQuestions: Find the gradient of y = x² − 3x at x = 2.

differentiation.hint: Focus on calculating the rate of change or slope of a curve (dy/dx).

integration.name: Integration
integration.subject: Coordinate & Calculus
clues: I am the reverse process of differentiation.
I find the area under a curve between two limits.
My power rule: ∫xⁿ dx = xⁿ⁺¹/(n+1) + C.
The constant C in my indefinite form is called the constant of integration.
The definite form of me uses limits a and b to give a numerical area.

educationalInfo.definition: Integration is the reverse of differentiation. Indefinite: ∫f(x)dx = F(x)+C. Definite: ∫[a,b]f(x)dx = F(b)−F(a).
educationalInfo.commonMistakes: Forgetting +C in indefinite integration. Using wrong limits in definite integration.
educationalInfo.funFact: Archimedes calculated the area of a parabolic segment using exhaustion: a precursor to integration: 2000 years before Newton.

integration.hint: Focus on finding the area under a curve or the anti-derivative.

differential_equations.name: Differential Equations
differential_equations.subject: Coordinate & Calculus
clues: I am an equation involving a function and its derivatives.
My simplest type is separable: variables can be separated to opposite sides.
dy/dx = ky describes exponential growth or decay.
I model physical systems: heat flow, population growth, electrical circuits.
Newton's law of cooling is a classic example of me.

educationalInfo.definition: An equation relating a function with one or more of its derivatives.
examples: dy/dx = 3x²: integrate both sides → y = x³ + C
educationalInfo.commonMistakes: Forgetting the constant of integration. Not applying the initial condition to find the specific solution.
educationalInfo.funFact: Maxwell's equations, which describe all electromagnetic phenomena, are a system of differential equations discovered in 1865.
practiceQuestions: Solve dy/dx = 4x, given y=3 when x=0.
Solve the separable equation dy/dx = y.

differential_equations.hint: Recall that Differential Equations refers to: An equation relating a function with one or more of its derivatives.

inverse_trigonometry.name: Inverse Trigonometry
inverse_trigonometry.subject: Coordinate & Calculus
clues: I find the angle when given a trigonometric ratio.
sin⁻¹(0.5) = 30° is a simple example of me.
My notation uses a superscript −1 or the prefix 'arc'.
I have restricted domains to ensure single-valued outputs.
arctan(1) = 45° because tan(45°) = 1.

educationalInfo.definition: Inverse trigonometric functions find the angle whose sine, cosine, or tangent equals a given value.
educationalInfo.commonMistakes: Ignoring restricted domains: arcsin only gives values in [−90°,90°]. Calculator mode (deg vs rad).
educationalInfo.funFact: Inverse trig functions are used in robotics to calculate joint angles from end-effector positions: inverse kinematics.

inverse_trigonometry.hint: Recall that Inverse Trigonometry refers to: Inverse trigonometric functions find the angle whose sine, cosine, or tangent equals a given value.

trigonometry.name: Trigonometry
trigonometry.subject: Coordinate & Calculus
clues: I study the relationships between angles and sides in triangles.
My three primary ratios are sine, cosine, and tangent.
The mnemonic SOH-CAH-TOA helps remember my definitions.
The Sine Rule and Cosine Rule extend me to non-right triangles.
I am essential in navigation, physics, and engineering.

educationalInfo.definition: The branch of mathematics studying relationships between angles and lengths of triangles.
educationalInfo.commonMistakes: Using SOH-CAH-TOA in non-right triangles without switching to sine/cosine rules.
educationalInfo.funFact: Ancient Babylonian astronomers used trigonometry-like tables 3700 years ago to track the planets.
practiceQuestions: In a right triangle with hypotenuse 10 and angle 30°, find the opposite side.
Use the cosine rule to find side a if b=5, c=7, A=60°.

trigonometry.hint: Recall that Trigonometry refers to: The branch of mathematics studying relationships between angles and lengths of triangles.

statistics.name: Statistics
statistics.subject: Data & Logic
clues: I am the science of collecting, organising, analysing, and interpreting data.
I use measures of central tendency and spread to summarise datasets.
Histograms, box plots, and scatter graphs are my visual tools.
I distinguish between census (whole population) and sample surveys.
The mean, median, and mode are my three main averages.

educationalInfo.definition: The discipline of collecting, organising, analysing, and interpreting numerical data to draw conclusions.
examples: Standard deviation measures spread around the mean
educationalInfo.commonMistakes: Using mean when data is skewed (median is better). Confusing frequency with relative frequency.
educationalInfo.funFact: Florence Nightingale pioneered the use of statistics in healthcare: her polar-area diagrams saved thousands of lives in the Crimean War.
practiceQuestions: What is the difference between mean and median?
Draw and interpret a back-to-back stem and leaf diagram.

statistics.hint: Recall that Statistics refers to: The discipline of collecting, organising, analysing, and interpreting numerical data to draw conclusions.

variation.name: Variation
variation.subject: Data & Logic
clues: I describe how two quantities change in relation to each other.
In my direct form, y ∝ x means y = kx for a constant k.
In my inverse form, y ∝ 1/x means y = k/x.
I can also involve powers: y ∝ x² means y = kx².
If y = 12 when x = 3 in direct variation, then k = 4, so y = 4x.

educationalInfo.definition: Direct variation: y = kx. Inverse variation: y = k/x. Joint variation: y = kxz. k is the constant of proportionality.
examples: y ∝ x: y=8 when x=2 → k=4, so y=4x
y ∝ 1/x: y=6 when x=2 → k=12, so y=12/x
educationalInfo.commonMistakes: Forgetting to find k before writing the equation. Confusing direct with inverse variation.
educationalInfo.funFact: Boyle's Law (pressure × volume = constant) is a perfect example of inverse variation in physics.
practiceQuestions: y varies directly as x. If y=15 when x=5, find y when x=8.
y is inversely proportional to x². If y=4 when x=3, find y when x=6.

variation.hint: Recall that Variation refers to: Direct variation: y = kx.

vocabulary.name: Vocabulary
vocabulary.subject: Data & Logic
clues: I represent the mathematical language itself: the meaning of the words we use.
I help students understand exam questions that use words like 'factorise', 'evaluate', or 'hence'.
Without me, a student may know a method but misread what is being asked.
I include terms like 'ascending', 'integer', 'consecutive', and 'congruent'.
Mathematical literacy: understanding my terms: is as important as numerical skill.

educationalInfo.definition: Mathematical vocabulary: the precise definitions of terms and command words used in mathematics.
educationalInfo.commonMistakes: Misreading 'factorise' as 'expand'. Confusing 'prove' with 'show' or 'verify'.
educationalInfo.funFact: The word 'algebra' comes from the Arabic 'al-jabr': from al-Khwarizmi's 9th-century book on balancing equations.
practiceQuestions: What does 'simplify' mean in a maths context?

vocabulary.hint: Recall that Vocabulary refers to: Mathematical vocabulary: the precise definitions of terms and command words used in mathematics.

algebraic_fraction.name: Algebraic Fractions
clues: I am a fraction containing variables in the numerator or denominator.
I can be simplified by factorizing and canceling common expressions.
I require a common denominator when adding or subtracting my terms.
To divide me, you multiply by the reciprocal of the divisor.
An example of me is: (x^2 - 4) / (x - 2), which simplifies to (x + 2).

educationalInfo.definition: A fraction whose numerator and/or denominator are algebraic expressions.
educationalInfo.commonMistakes: Canceling terms that are added rather than multiplied (e.g. trying to cancel 'x' in (x+2)/x to get 2).
educationalInfo.funFact: Simplifying algebraic fractions is key to solving rational equations and performing integral calculus.

algebraic_fraction.hint: Recall that Algebraic Fractions refers to: A fraction whose numerator and/or denominator are algebraic expressions.

even_numbers.name: Even Numbers
even_numbers.subject: Arithmetic
clues: I love making pairs of socks, shoes, and dance partners!
When you share me between 2 friends, everyone gets the exact same amount with 0 left over!
My last digit is always 0, 2, 4, 6, or 8!
Numbers like 2, 4, 6, 8, 10 belong to my family.
I am any whole number that can be divided by 2 with no remainder!
hints: Can be split into equal pairs.

educationalInfo.definition: Even numbers are integers divisible by 2 without leaving any remainder (0, 2, 4, 6, 8...).
educationalInfo.commonMistakes: Thinking 0 is not an even number (0 is even!).
educationalInfo.funFact: Adding two even numbers always gives another even number!

even_numbers.hint: Recall that even numbers are integers perfectly divisible by 2 with no remainder (ending in 0, 2, 4, 6, 8).

odd_numbers.name: Odd Numbers
odd_numbers.subject: Arithmetic
clues: When you pair us up, there is always 1 lonely item left over!
When you try to split me equally between 2 friends, 1 item is always left out!
My last digit is always 1, 3, 5, 7, or 9!
Numbers like 1, 3, 5, 7, 9 belong to my family.
I am any whole number that leaves a remainder of 1 when divided by 2!
hints: Leaves a remainder of 1 when divided by 2.

educationalInfo.definition: Odd numbers are integers that leave a remainder of 1 when divided by 2 (1, 3, 5, 7, 9...).
educationalInfo.commonMistakes: Thinking odd numbers cannot be prime numbers.
educationalInfo.funFact: Multiplying any odd number by another odd number always yields an odd number!

odd_numbers.hint: Recall that odd numbers leave a remainder of 1 when divided by 2 (ending in 1, 3, 5, 7, 9).

prime_numbers.name: Prime Number
prime_numbers.subject: Arithmetic
clues: I am a special number that cannot be made by multiplying smaller whole numbers together!
I have EXACTLY two factors: 1 and myself!
Numbers like 4, 6, 8, 9 cannot join me because they have extra multiplication partners.
Numbers 2, 3, 5, 7, and 11 are my best friends!
I am a whole number greater than 1 with exactly two factors: 1 and itself!

educationalInfo.definition: A whole number greater than 1 with exactly two positive divisors: 1 and itself.
educationalInfo.commonMistakes: Confusing prime numbers with odd numbers (e.g. 9 or 15 are odd but not prime). Believing 1 is a prime number.
educationalInfo.funFact: The number 2 is the only even prime number. All other prime numbers are odd!
practiceQuestions: What is the next prime number after 19?

prime_numbers.hint: Focus on numbers greater than 1 that have exactly two factors: 1 and themselves (e.g. 2, 3, 5, 7, 11).

composite_numbers.name: Composite Number
composite_numbers.subject: Arithmetic
clues: I am a team number built by multiplying smaller whole numbers together!
I have MORE than two factors (multiplication partners)!
You can arrange my count into equal rows or box grids, like a 2x3 egg box.
Numbers like 4, 6, 8, 9, 10 belong to my team!
I am any positive whole number greater than 1 that has more than two factors!

educationalInfo.definition: A positive integer that has at least one positive divisor other than 1 and itself.
educationalInfo.commonMistakes: Thinking 1 is composite: it is neither prime nor composite.
educationalInfo.funFact: Every composite number can be uniquely expressed as a product of prime numbers, known as its prime factorisation.
practiceQuestions: Why is 1 neither prime nor composite?

composite_numbers.hint: Think of positive integers greater than 1 that have more than two positive factors (e.g. 4, 6, 8, 9).

factor.name: Factor
factor.subject: Arithmetic
clues: I am a smaller number that fits inside a bigger number perfectly!
I divide into a target number cleanly with no remainder left over!
For 12, my family members are 1, 2, 3, 4, 6, and 12!
I tell you how many equal rows you can make with a set of tiles.
I am a whole number that divides another number exactly without leaving a remainder.
hints: Always smaller than or equal to the number.
1 is a factor of every number.

educationalInfo.definition: A factor is a number that divides another number completely without leaving a remainder.
educationalInfo.commonMistakes: Confusing factors (smaller) with multiples (larger).
educationalInfo.funFact: Number 1 is a factor of every single whole number!

factor.hint: Focus on numbers that divide evenly into another number with zero remainder.

multiple.name: Multiple
multiple.subject: Arithmetic
clues: I am what you get when you skip-count by a number!
I grow bigger and bigger forever as you multiply by 1, 2, 3, 4...
Skip-counting by 5 gives my family: 5, 10, 15, 20, 25...
I tell you when a clock chime or bus arrives on a regular repeating schedule!
I am the result of multiplying a whole number by any counting number!

educationalInfo.definition: A multiple is the product obtained by multiplying a number by any whole integer.
educationalInfo.commonMistakes: Thinking a number has a limited count of multiples.
educationalInfo.funFact: Every number has an infinite number of multiples!

multiple.hint: Think of numbers in the multiplication table of a given number.

divisible_by_2.name: Divisible by 2
divisible_by_2.subject: Arithmetic
clues: I am a divisibility rule for sharing things evenly between 2 friends!
You only need to look at my very last digit to check me!
If a number ends in 0, 2, 4, 6, or 8, it passes my test!
Numbers like 14, 28, and 100 pass my rule effortlessly.
I am the rule where any number ending in an even digit (0, 2, 4, 6, 8) can be divided by 2!

educationalInfo.definition: A number is divisible by 2 if its last digit is an even number (0, 2, 4, 6, 8).
educationalInfo.commonMistakes: Checking the first digit instead of the last digit.
educationalInfo.funFact: This is the fastest divisibility test in mathematics!

divisible_by_2.hint: Recall that Divisible by 2 refers to: A number is divisible by 2 if its last digit is an even number (0, 2, 4, 6, 8).

divisible_by_3.name: Divisible by 3
divisible_by_3.subject: Arithmetic
clues: I am a magic rule where you ADD UP all the digits of a number!
If the sum of all digits can be divided by 3, the whole big number passes!
For 123, 1+2+3 = 6, and 6 is in the 3 times table, so 123 passes!
You don't need long division: just add the digits together!
I am the rule where a number is divisible by 3 if the sum of its digits is a multiple of 3!
hints: If sum is in 3 times table, it passes.
Does not depend on last digit alone.

educationalInfo.definition: A number is divisible by 3 if the sum of its digits is divisible by 3.
educationalInfo.commonMistakes: Thinking odd ending numbers are automatically divisible by 3.
educationalInfo.funFact: Summing digits works because 10 = 9 + 1, and 9 is divisible by 3!

divisible_by_3.hint: Recall that Divisible by 3 refers to: A number is divisible by 3 if the sum of its digits is divisible by 3.

divisible_by_5.name: Divisible by 5
divisible_by_5.subject: Arithmetic
clues: I am a super easy rule that you use when counting nickel coins or 5-point stars!
You only need to glance at the very last digit at the end of the number!
If the last digit is 0 or 5, the number passes my test instantly!
Numbers like 15, 40, 85, and 500 pass my rule!
I am the rule where any number ending in 0 or 5 is divisible by 5!

educationalInfo.definition: A number is divisible by 5 if its last digit is either 0 or 5.
educationalInfo.commonMistakes: Thinking numbers ending in 5 are the only ones (0 also counts!).
educationalInfo.funFact: Every multiple of 10 is automatically divisible by 5!

divisible_by_5.hint: Recall that Divisible by 5 refers to: A number is divisible by 5 if its last digit is either 0 or 5.

divisible_by_9.name: Divisible by 9
divisible_by_9.subject: Arithmetic
clues: I am a digit-sum magic rule just like the rule for 3, but for a bigger number!
Add all the digits together: if the total sum is in the 9 times table, it passes!
For 729, 7+2+9 = 18, and 18 can be divided by 9, so 729 passes!
It works for huge numbers like 9,999 or 1,800 without doing long division!
I am the rule where a number is divisible by 9 if the sum of its digits is a multiple of 9!

educationalInfo.definition: A number is divisible by 9 if the sum of its digits is divisible by 9.
educationalInfo.commonMistakes: Confusing divisible by 3 with divisible by 9.
educationalInfo.funFact: Every number divisible by 9 is also divisible by 3!

divisible_by_9.hint: Recall that Divisible by 9 refers to: A number is divisible by 9 if the sum of its digits is divisible by 9.

ones_place.name: Ones
ones_place.subject: Arithmetic
clues: I am the rightmost spot in a number where single digits live!
I count single individual items from 0 to 9.
In the number 345, the digit 5 sits in my spot!
Before you add tens or hundreds, you always start adding from my spot!
I am the place value representing single units (1s) at the far right of a whole number!
hints: Far right position in whole numbers.

educationalInfo.definition: The ones place represents individual units (10^0 = 1) at the rightmost position of a whole number.
examples: In 42, 2 is in the ones place
educationalInfo.commonMistakes: Reading place values from left to right instead of right to left.
educationalInfo.funFact: Ones place is the starting anchor for all place value calculations!

ones_place.hint: Look at the last digit on the far right of an integer (the 1s column).

tens_place.name: Tens
tens_place.subject: Arithmetic
clues: I am the spot just to the left of the ones place!
Each digit in my spot is worth groups of 10 items (like 10, 20, 30...).
In the number 345, the digit 4 sits in my spot and is worth 40!
When you collect 10 single ones, they combine into 1 in my spot!
I am the place value representing groups of ten (10s) in a number!

educationalInfo.definition: The tens place represents groups of ten (10^1 = 10), sitting immediately to the left of the ones place.
examples: In 54, 5 is in the tens place (50)
educationalInfo.commonMistakes: Forgetting that digit 5 in tens place means 50.
educationalInfo.funFact: Our decimal system is built around powers of 10!

tens_place.hint: Look at the second digit from the right (representing groups of 10).

hundreds_place.name: Hundreds
hundreds_place.subject: Arithmetic
clues: I am the spot three places from the right in a 3-digit number!
Each digit in my spot is worth bundles of 100 items!
In the number 345, the digit 3 sits in my spot and is worth 300!
10 tens grouped together make 1 in my spot!
I am the place value representing groups of hundred (100s) in a number!

educationalInfo.definition: The hundreds place represents groups of one hundred (10^2 = 100).
examples: In 345, 3 is in the hundreds place (300)
educationalInfo.commonMistakes: Confusing hundreds with hundredths.
educationalInfo.funFact: 1 hundred equals 10 tens or 100 ones!

hundreds_place.hint: Recall that Hundreds refers to: The hundreds place represents groups of one hundred (10^2 = 100).

thousands_place.name: Thousands
thousands_place.subject: Arithmetic
clues: I am the spot sitting just to the left of a comma in 4-digit numbers!
Each digit in my spot is worth giant bundles of 1,000 items!
In the number 2,345, the digit 2 sits in my spot and is worth 2,000!
10 hundreds grouped together make 1 in my spot!
I am the place value representing groups of thousand (1,000s) in a number!

educationalInfo.definition: The thousands place represents groups of one thousand (10^3 = 1000).
examples: In 2,500, 2 is in the thousands place
educationalInfo.commonMistakes: Miscounting positions when zeros are present.
educationalInfo.funFact: 1 thousand equals 10 hundreds or 1,000 ones!

thousands_place.hint: Look at the 4th digit from the right, representing 1,000s.

greater_than.name: Greater Than (>)
greater_than.subject: Arithmetic
clues: I am a mathematical comparison concept used when looking at two values!
I state that the first number is LARGER in value than the second number.
My symbol '>' opens its wide hungry mouth toward the left number!
Comparing 10 points to 4 points on a leaderboard.
The 'Greater Than' symbol (>) indicates that the value on the left is strictly larger than the value on the right.
hints: Alligator mouth eats the bigger number.

educationalInfo.definition: The greater than symbol (>) indicates that the value on the left is larger than the value on the right.
educationalInfo.commonMistakes: Confusing > (greater than) with < (less than).
educationalInfo.funFact: Think of > as an arrow pointing to the smaller number!

greater_than.hint: Recall that the symbol > points to the smaller number and opens wide toward the larger value.

less_than.name: Less Than (<)
less_than.subject: Arithmetic
clues: I am a mathematical comparison concept used between numbers.
I state that the first number is SMALLER in value than the second number.
My symbol '<' points its narrow sharp tip toward the left number!
Comparing ₹50 in your pocket to a toy that costs ₹100.
The 'Less Than' symbol (<) indicates that the value on the left is strictly smaller than the value on the right.
hints: Points to the smaller left number.

educationalInfo.definition: The less than symbol (<) indicates that the value on the left is smaller than the value on the right.
educationalInfo.commonMistakes: Confusing < with >.
educationalInfo.funFact: The symbol '<' actually resembles an 'L' for 'Less'!

less_than.hint: Recall that the symbol < points left toward the smaller value.

equal_to.name: Equal To (=)
equal_to.subject: Arithmetic
clues: I am a symbol of perfect balance between two amounts or expressions.
I state that both sides have EXACTLY the same value!
I am written with two parallel horizontal lines '='.
When 2 + 3 has the exact same total as 5 on a balance scale.
The 'Equal To' symbol (=) indicates that two expressions have identical values.
hints: Both sides have the exact same value.

educationalInfo.definition: The equal sign (=) shows that two expressions have identical values.
educationalInfo.commonMistakes: Thinking '=' means 'calculate the answer' rather than 'balanced equivalence'.
educationalInfo.funFact: The '=' symbol was invented in 1557 by Robert Recorde because no two things could be more equal than parallel lines!

equal_to.hint: Think of two mathematical expressions that have identical quantitative values (=).

ascending_order.name: Ascending Order
ascending_order.subject: Arithmetic
clues: I am a method of arranging a list of multiple numbers!
I arrange a sequence starting from the smallest number and stepping up to the largest!
Unlike descending order, my numbers get bigger as you read from left to right!
Line up students in a class by height from shortest to tallest.
Ascending order means arranging numbers in order from smallest to largest.

educationalInfo.definition: Ascending order arranges numbers starting from the smallest value up to the largest value.
educationalInfo.commonMistakes: Mixing up ascending (increasing) and descending (decreasing).
educationalInfo.funFact: 'Ascend' means to go up or climb!

ascending_order.hint: Arrange numbers from smallest to largest value.

proper_fraction.name: Proper Fraction
proper_fraction.subject: Arithmetic
clues: I describe a fractional amount when comparing parts to a whole unit.
My total value is strictly LESS than 1 whole unit!
My top number (numerator) is strictly smaller than my bottom number (denominator).
Eating 3 slices out of an 8-slice pizza (3/8).
A proper fraction is a fraction where the numerator is smaller than the denominator (e.g. 3/4).

educationalInfo.definition: A proper fraction has a numerator that is smaller than its denominator, making its value less than 1.
educationalInfo.commonMistakes: Thinking fractions are always proper.
educationalInfo.funFact: Proper fractions represent a true part of a single whole!

proper_fraction.hint: Focus on fractions where the numerator is smaller than the denominator (e.g. 3/4).

improper_fraction.name: Improper Fraction
improper_fraction.subject: Arithmetic
clues: I am a fraction format used in math calculations.
My total value is GREATER than or EQUAL to 1 whole unit!
My top number (numerator) is greater than or equal to my bottom number (denominator), written as a single fraction without a whole number beside it.
Expressing 7 quarter slices of pizza as 7/4.
An improper fraction is a fraction where the numerator is greater than or equal to the denominator (e.g. 7/4).
hints: Numerator is greater than or equal to denominator.

educationalInfo.definition: An improper fraction has a numerator greater than or equal to its denominator.
educationalInfo.commonMistakes: Thinking improper fractions are 'wrong' (they are completely valid!).
educationalInfo.funFact: Every improper fraction can be rewritten as a mixed fraction!

improper_fraction.hint: Focus on fractions where the numerator is greater than or equal to the denominator (e.g. 7/4).

mixed_fraction.name: Mixed Fraction
mixed_fraction.subject: Arithmetic
clues: I am a way of writing fractional quantities greater than 1.
I combine a whole number and a proper fraction side-by-side!
I am written with a big whole number on the left followed by a smaller fraction (e.g. 1 3/4).
Saying a recipe needs 2 and a half cups of flour (2 1/2).
A mixed fraction (or mixed number) consists of a whole number combined with a proper fraction (e.g. 1 3/4).
hints: Combines a whole number and a fraction.

educationalInfo.definition: A mixed fraction (or mixed number) combines a whole number and a proper fraction.
educationalInfo.commonMistakes: Multiplying the whole number and fraction instead of adding them.
educationalInfo.funFact: 2 1/2 is equal to the improper fraction 5/2!

mixed_fraction.hint: Think of a combination of a whole number and a proper fraction (e.g. 2 1/2).

equivalent_fraction.name: Equivalent Fraction
equivalent_fraction.subject: Arithmetic
clues: I am a relationship between two different-looking fractions!
Even though my numbers on top and bottom look different, my overall value is EXACTLY the same!
You get me by multiplying or dividing the top and bottom of a fraction by the same number (e.g. 1/2 = 2/4 = 4/8).
1 out of 2 slices of a large pizza is the same amount of food as 2 out of 4 slices of a small pizza.
Equivalent fractions are fractions that have different numerators and denominators but represent the exact same value (e.g. 1/2 and 2/4).
hints: Made by multiplying top & bottom by the same number.

educationalInfo.definition: Equivalent fractions represent equal values or proportions even if their numerators and denominators differ.
educationalInfo.commonMistakes: Adding the same number to top and bottom (you must multiply or divide!).
educationalInfo.funFact: There are infinitely many equivalent fractions for any single fraction!

equivalent_fraction.hint: Recall fractions that have equal value even though their numerators and denominators differ (e.g. 1/2 = 2/4).

tenths.name: Tenths
tenths.subject: Arithmetic
clues: I am a decimal place value position to the right of the decimal point!
I sit at the VERY FIRST position immediately after the decimal dot!
My value represents dividing 1 whole into 10 equal parts (1/10 = 0.1).
In 0.45 meters, my position holds the 4 (0.4 m).
The tenths place is the first position to the right of the decimal point, representing 1/10th units.
hints: First digit after the decimal point.

educationalInfo.definition: The tenths place is the first position to the right of the decimal point, representing tenths (1/10 or 0.1).
examples: In 0.7, 7 is in the tenths place
educationalInfo.commonMistakes: Confusing tens (left of dot) with tenths (right of dot).
educationalInfo.funFact: 10 tenths make 1 whole unit!

tenths.hint: Look at the first digit immediately to the right of the decimal point (1/10th).

hundredths.name: Hundredths
hundredths.subject: Arithmetic
clues: I am a decimal place value position used when measuring smaller precision.
I sit at the SECOND position to the right of the decimal point.
My value represents dividing 1 whole into 100 equal parts (1/100 = 0.01).
In money prices like ₹12.75, my position holds the 5 paise.
The hundredths place is the second position to the right of the decimal point, representing 1/100th units.
hints: Second digit after the decimal point.

educationalInfo.definition: The hundredths place is the second position to the right of the decimal point (1/100 or 0.01).
examples: In 0.25, 5 is in the hundredths place
educationalInfo.commonMistakes: Thinking 0.05 is bigger than 0.5.
educationalInfo.funFact: 10 hundredths equal 1 tenth!

hundredths.hint: Look at the second digit to the right of the decimal point (1/100th).

thousandths.name: Thousandths
thousandths.subject: Arithmetic
clues: I am a decimal place value position used for ultra-high precision.
I sit at the THIRD position to the right of the decimal point.
My value represents dividing 1 whole into 1,000 equal parts (1/1000 = 0.001).
Used in scientific laboratories to measure 0.005 grams of chemical.
The thousandths place is the third position to the right of the decimal point, representing 1/1000th units.
hints: Third digit after the decimal point.

educationalInfo.definition: The thousandths place is the third position to the right of the decimal point (1/1000 or 0.001).
examples: In 0.123, 3 is in the thousandths place
educationalInfo.commonMistakes: Miscounting decimal places.
educationalInfo.funFact: 1,000 thousandths make 1 whole unit!

thousandths.hint: Look at the third digit to the right of the decimal point (1/1000th).

decimal_number_concept.name: Decimal Number
decimal_number_concept.subject: Arithmetic
clues: I am a full numerical format used to show precise quantities.
Unlike individual place value names, I am the ENTIRE number format that uses a dot separator!
I combine whole numbers on the left of a dot with fractional place values on the right.
You see me on digital thermometers showing 98.6°F.
A decimal number is a number expressed in base-10 system using a decimal point to separate whole and fractional parts.

educationalInfo.definition: A decimal number is a number that uses a decimal point to represent whole numbers and fractions of ten.
educationalInfo.commonMistakes: Ignoring the position of the decimal point.
educationalInfo.funFact: Decimals allow us to write any fraction using standard place value digits!

decimal_number_concept.hint: Think of quantities written with a decimal point to represent fractional parts of 1.

fraction_form.name: Fraction
fraction_form.subject: Arithmetic
clues: I am a way of representing proportional parts of a whole.
I use a top number (numerator) stacked over a bottom number (denominator) separated by a bar.
I am written like a/b, without using a dot, '%' sign, or ':' colon.
Recipes calling for 3/4 cup of sugar.
A fraction represents a numerical part of a whole expressed as numerator over denominator (a/b).

educationalInfo.definition: A fraction expresses a part of a whole as a numerator divided by a denominator.
educationalInfo.commonMistakes: Thinking top and bottom can be added directly when adding fractions.
educationalInfo.funFact: Fraction lines were introduced by Indian mathematicians!

fraction_form.hint: Recall that Fraction refers to: A fraction expresses a part of a whole as a numerator divided by a denominator.

decimal_form.name: Decimal
decimal_form.subject: Arithmetic
clues: I am a numerical format used to show non-whole values.
I express fractional values using a single dot point separator!
I convert parts of 10, 100, 1000 using place value, without using a slash bar or '%' symbol.
Digital calculators displaying 0.75.
A decimal is a number in the base-10 system using a decimal point.

educationalInfo.definition: A decimal represents fractional quantities using place values of base 10.
educationalInfo.commonMistakes: Adding decimal trailing zeros incorrectly.
educationalInfo.funFact: Decimals make calculating with fractions much faster on computers!

decimal_form.hint: Recall that Decimal refers to: A decimal represents fractional quantities using place values of base 10.

percentage_form.name: Percentage
percentage_form.subject: Arithmetic
clues: I am a popular mathematical format used to compare proportions and rates!
I ALWAYS express a ratio or part out of a fixed base of 100!
I use the special percent symbol '%' right after the number.
Store discounts offering 50% off or exam scores of 85%.
A percentage is a number or ratio expressed as a fraction of 100, using the '%' symbol.

educationalInfo.definition: A percentage is a ratio that compares a number to 100, represented by %.
educationalInfo.commonMistakes: Thinking percentages cannot be greater than 100% (they can!).
educationalInfo.funFact: The word 'percent' comes from Latin 'per centum', meaning 'by the hundred'!

percentage_form.hint: Recall that percent means per 100: a ratio expressed out of 100.

ratio_form.name: Ratio
ratio_form.subject: Arithmetic
clues: I am a mathematical comparison between two quantities!
I compare two numbers directly to show how many times one value contains another.
I am written with a colon symbol ':' separating the two quantities (e.g. 2:3).
Mixing paint using 2 buckets of blue paint to 3 buckets of yellow paint (2:3).
A ratio is a quantitative comparison showing the relative sizes of two or more values (a:b).

educationalInfo.definition: A ratio compares two quantities using a colon (a:b) to show their relative sizes.
educationalInfo.commonMistakes: Reversing the order of quantities in a ratio.
educationalInfo.funFact: Ratios are used in baking recipes to scale ingredients perfectly!

ratio_form.hint: Think about comparing two quantities by division (written a:b or a/b).

arithmetic_pattern.name: Arithmetic Pattern
arithmetic_pattern.subject: Arithmetic
clues: I am a sequence of numbers following a predictable rule!
You get the next number by ADDING or SUBTRACTING the same constant number each step!
The difference between any two adjacent terms is always identical (common difference).
Climbing a staircase where every step increases your height by 20 cm.
An arithmetic pattern is a sequence of numbers with a constant common difference added or subtracted each term.
hints: Adds or subtracts a constant number.

educationalInfo.definition: An arithmetic pattern (sequence) is a list of numbers where each term increases or decreases by a constant common difference.
educationalInfo.commonMistakes: Multiplying instead of adding.
educationalInfo.funFact: House numbers on a street often follow an arithmetic pattern of +2!

arithmetic_pattern.hint: Recall that Arithmetic Pattern refers to: An arithmetic pattern (sequence) is a list of numbers where each term increases or decreases by a constant common difference.

geometric_pattern.name: Geometric Pattern
geometric_pattern.subject: Arithmetic
clues: I am a number sequence that grows or shrinks according to a rule.
You get the next number by MULTIPLYING or DIVIDING by the same constant factor each step!
My numbers grow very rapidly (exponentially) because each term multiplies the previous one.
Bacteria doubling in population every hour (1, 2, 4, 8, 16...).
A geometric pattern is a sequence of numbers where each term is found by multiplying the previous term by a constant factor.

educationalInfo.definition: A geometric pattern is a sequence where each term is multiplied by a constant ratio to get the next term.
educationalInfo.commonMistakes: Adding instead of multiplying.
educationalInfo.funFact: Cell division in biology follows a geometric pattern of ×2!

geometric_pattern.hint: Recall that Geometric Pattern refers to: A geometric pattern is a sequence where each term is multiplied by a constant ratio to get the next term.
